reminder: A metric is an ultrametric when $d(x,z)\le\max(d(x,y),d(y,z))$ for all points $x,y,z$.
definition: A [metric](c:metric-space) $d$ on a set $X$, with values in the [real numbers](c:real-number), is an ultrametric when $d(x,z)\le\max(d(x,y),d(y,z))$ for all $x,y,z\in X$. In every triangle of an ultrametric space, the two longest sides have equal length.
examples: The $p$-adic distance $d(x,y)=|x-y|_p$ on $\mathbb{Q}$ is an ultrametric.
The discrete metric, with $d(x,y)=1$ for $x\ne y$, is an ultrametric, because $y$ differs from $x$ or from $z$ when $x\ne z$.
On infinite binary sequences, $d(x,y)=2^{-n}$, where $n$ is the first place where $x$ and $y$ differ, is an ultrametric.
Non-example: the usual distance on $\mathbb{R}$ is not an ultrametric, because $d(0,2)=2$ is larger than $\max(d(0,1),d(1,2))=1$.

steps: Let $d$ be an ultrametric on $X$ and take $x,y,z\in X$.
The numbers $d(x,y)$ and $d(y,z)$ are not negative, so the larger of the two is at most their sum.
So $d(x,z)\le\max(d(x,y),d(y,z))\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$, which is the triangle inequality.
Hence $d$ is a [metric](c:metric-space); the ultrametric case adds that the larger term can replace the sum.
links.why: It shows that every ultrametric space is a metric space with a stronger triangle inequality.

reminder: The Ising model puts a spin $\pm1$ on each vertex of a graph, with an energy that depends on neighboring spins.
definition: Let $\Lambda$ be a finite [graph](c:graph), for example a box in the lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$. A configuration is a function $\sigma:\Lambda\to\{-1,+1\}$ with [Hamiltonian](c:hamiltonian) $H(\sigma)=-J\sum_{i\sim j}\sigma_i\sigma_j-h\sum_i\sigma_i$, where the first sum runs over the edges of $\Lambda$. At inverse temperature $\beta$, the model is the [Gibbs distribution](c:gibbs-distribution) $\mathbb{P}(\sigma)=e^{-\beta H(\sigma)}/Z$, where $Z$ is the [partition function](c:partition-function).
examples: The chain $\{1,\dots,n\}$ with an edge between each pair of neighbors is the one-dimensional Ising model.
The square lattice $\mathbb{Z}^2$ with $h=0$ and $J>0$ has a phase transition at a positive critical temperature (Onsager).
For $J>0$, neighbors with equal spins have lower energy (ferromagnet); for $J<0$, they have higher energy (antiferromagnet).
Non-example: a model whose spins are unit vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$ is the Heisenberg model, because Ising spins take only the two values $\pm1$.

steps: A [Gibbs distribution](c:gibbs-distribution) on a finite set $\Omega$ with energy $H$ gives $\omega$ the probability $e^{-\beta H(\omega)}/Z$.
Take $\Omega=\{-1,+1\}^\Lambda$, the set of spin configurations on the graph $\Lambda$.
Take $H$ to be the Ising energy $-J\sum_{i\sim j}\sigma_i\sigma_j-h\sum_i\sigma_i$.
The Gibbs distribution of this pair is the Ising model at inverse temperature $\beta$.
links.why: It shows that the Ising model is one choice of state space and energy inside the general Gibbs framework.

reminder: The $J$-homomorphism sends a class in $\pi_k(SO(n))$ to a class in $\pi_{n+k}(S^n)$ by the Hopf construction.
definition: For $k,n\ge1$, the $J$-homomorphism is the group homomorphism $J:\pi_k(SO(n))\to\pi_{n+k}(S^n)$ from the [homotopy groups](c:homotopy-group) of the [special orthogonal group](c:special-orthogonal-group) to those of [spheres](c:sphere). It sends the class of a map $\alpha:S^k\to SO(n)$ to the Hopf construction of $S^k\times S^{n-1}\to S^{n-1}$, $(x,y)\mapsto\alpha(x)y$, which is a map $S^{n+k}=S^k*S^{n-1}\to\Sigma S^{n-1}=S^n$. These maps are compatible with $n\mapsto n+1$ and give a stable map $J:\pi_k(SO)\to\pi_k^s$ into the stable [homotopy groups of spheres](c:homotopy-groups-of-spheres).
examples: For $k=1$ and $n=2$, the generator of $\pi_1(SO(2))\cong\mathbb{Z}$ goes to the class of the Hopf map in $\pi_3(S^2)\cong\mathbb{Z}$.
The stable map $J:\pi_1(SO)\cong\mathbb{Z}/2\to\pi_1^s\cong\mathbb{Z}/2$ is an isomorphism.
The image of $J:\pi_3(SO)\cong\mathbb{Z}\to\pi_3^s\cong\mathbb{Z}/24$ is all of $\mathbb{Z}/24$.
Non-example: the map $\pi_k(SO(n))\to\pi_k(S^{n-1})$ given by $A\mapsto Ae_1$ is not the $J$-homomorphism, because its target is $\pi_k(S^{n-1})$, not $\pi_{n+k}(S^n)$.

examples: In $\mathbb{R}^n$ the curvature is zero, so the Jacobi fields along a line are $J(t)=a+tb$ with constant vectors $a,b$.
Along every geodesic $\gamma$, the fields $\dot\gamma$ and $t\dot\gamma$ are Jacobi fields.
On the unit sphere, along a unit-speed geodesic $\gamma$, the field $J(t)=\sin(t)E(t)$ is a Jacobi field when $E$ is a parallel unit field normal to $\gamma$.

reminder: A Kan complex is a simplicial set in which every horn has a filler.
definition: A [simplicial set](c:simplicial-set) $X$ is a Kan complex when, for all $n\ge1$ and $0\le k\le n$, every map $\Lambda^n_k\to X$ extends to a map $\Delta^n\to X$. Here the [horn](c:horn) $\Lambda^n_k$ is the boundary of the [simplex](c:simplex) $\Delta^n$ with its interior and its $k$-th face removed.
examples: The singular simplicial set $\mathrm{Sing}(T)$ of a topological space $T$ is a Kan complex.
The nerve of a [groupoid](c:groupoid) is a Kan complex.
Every simplicial group is a Kan complex.
Non-example: the nerve of the poset $0<1$ is not a Kan complex, because the horn $\Lambda^2_0$ with vertices $(0,1,0)$ has no filler, as $0\le1\le0$ is false.

steps: A [quasi-category](c:quasi-category) is a simplicial set in which every inner horn $\Lambda^n_k$ with $0<k<n$ has a filler.
Let $X$ be a Kan complex, so every horn of $X$ has a filler.
The inner horns are horns, so every inner horn of $X$ has a filler.
Hence $X$ is a quasi-category; the Kan case adds fillers for the outer horns with $k=0$ and $k=n$.
links.why: It shows that Kan complexes are the quasi-categories in which every morphism is invertible.

reminder: A Kempe chain is a connected component of the subgraph on the vertices that have one of two given colors.
definition: Let $c$ be a proper [coloring](c:graph-coloring) of a [graph](c:graph) $G$ and let $a\ne b$ be two colors. A Kempe chain is a [connected component](c:connected-component) of the [induced subgraph](c:induced-subgraph) of $G$ on the vertices with color $a$ or $b$. Swapping $a$ and $b$ on one Kempe chain gives another proper coloring.
examples: In a path whose vertices have colors $1,2,1,2$, the whole path is one Kempe chain for the colors $1$ and $2$.
In the 4-cycle $v_1v_2v_3v_4$ with colors $1,2,3,2$, the Kempe chain of colors $1,2$ through $v_1$ is $\{v_1,v_2,v_4\}$, and swapping gives the proper coloring $2,1,3,1$.
Non-example: in a path with colors $1,2,3,1,2$, the set of the four vertices with colors $1$ and $2$ is not a Kempe chain, because it is not connected.

reminder: The Kerr–Newman metric is the exact solution of the Einstein–Maxwell equations for a rotating, electrically charged black hole.
definition: In Boyer-Lindquist coordinates $(t,r,\theta,\varphi)$ and units with $G=c=4\pi\varepsilon_0=1$, the Kerr–Newman metric with mass $M$, spin parameter $a$ and charge $Q$ is $ds^2=-\frac{\Delta}{\rho^2}(dt-a\sin^2\theta\,d\varphi)^2+\frac{\sin^2\theta}{\rho^2}((r^2+a^2)d\varphi-a\,dt)^2+\frac{\rho^2}{\Delta}dr^2+\rho^2d\theta^2$, with $\rho^2=r^2+a^2\cos^2\theta$ and $\Delta=r^2-2Mr+a^2+Q^2$. It is a [Lorentzian](c:lorentzian-manifold) metric that solves the [Einstein field equations](c:einstein-field-equations) together with an electromagnetic field of charge $Q$.
examples: With $Q=0$ the metric is the Kerr metric of a rotating black hole without charge.
With $a=0$ the metric is the Reissner–Nordström metric of a charged black hole without rotation.
Non-example: the Schwarzschild–de Sitter metric is not a Kerr–Newman metric, because it has a cosmological constant $\Lambda\ne0$.

steps: Start with the Kerr–Newman metric with parameters $M$, $a$ and $Q$.
Put $Q=0$, so that $\Delta=r^2-2Mr+a^2$.
The metric is then the Kerr metric with mass $M$ and spin parameter $a$.
links.why: It shows that the Kerr–Newman family adds electric charge to the Kerr family.

steps: Start with the Kerr–Newman metric and put $a=0$, so that $\rho^2=r^2$ and $\Delta=r^2-2Mr+Q^2$.
The cross terms in $d\varphi\,dt$ vanish, and the metric becomes $-f\,dt^2+f^{-1}dr^2+r^2(d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2)$.
Here $f=1-2M/r+Q^2/r^2$, which is the Reissner–Nordström metric.
links.why: It shows that the Kerr–Newman family adds rotation to the Reissner–Nordström family.

steps: Start with the Kerr–Newman metric and put $a=0$ and $Q=0$.
Then $\rho^2=r^2$ and $\Delta=r^2-2Mr$, so $\Delta/\rho^2=1-2M/r$.
The metric becomes $-(1-2M/r)dt^2+(1-2M/r)^{-1}dr^2+r^2(d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2)$, the Schwarzschild metric.
links.why: It shows that the Schwarzschild metric is the case of a black hole with no spin and no charge.

reminder: An L-function is a Dirichlet series with an Euler product that continues to a meromorphic function.
definition: An $L$-function is a [Dirichlet series](c:dirichlet-series) $L(s)=\sum_{n\ge1}a_nn^{-s}$ with an [Euler product](c:euler-product) over the [primes](c:prime-number), $L(s)=\prod_pL_p(p^{-s})$, for $\mathrm{Re}(s)$ large, which extends to a [meromorphic function](c:meromorphic-function) on $\mathbb{C}$. For a [Dirichlet character](c:dirichlet-character) $\chi$ this gives $L(s,\chi)=\sum_{n\ge1}\chi(n)n^{-s}=\prod_p(1-\chi(p)p^{-s})^{-1}$. Other $L$-functions come from number fields, elliptic curves and automorphic forms.
examples: For a nontrivial Dirichlet character $\chi$, the function $L(s,\chi)$ extends to an entire function.
The Riemann zeta function $\zeta(s)=\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-s}=\prod_p(1-p^{-s})^{-1}$ is an $L$-function with a simple pole at $s=1$.
The [Hasse–Weil L-function](c:hasse-weil-l-function) of an elliptic curve over $\mathbb{Q}$ is an $L$-function, and modularity gives its continuation.
Non-example: the series $1+6^{-s}$ has no Euler product, because $a_6=1$ while $a_2a_3=0$.

steps: Take the trivial Dirichlet character, with $\chi(n)=1$ for all $n$.
Then $L(s,\chi)=\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-s}$, with Euler product $\prod_p(1-p^{-s})^{-1}$.
This is the [Riemann zeta function](c:riemann-zeta-function), which continues to a meromorphic function with a simple pole at $s=1$.
links.why: It shows that the zeta function is the simplest L-function, and that other L-functions twist it with characters.

steps: Take an elliptic curve $E$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ and count its points modulo each prime $p$.
These counts give a local factor $L_p(p^{-s})$ at each prime $p$.
The product of all local factors is a Dirichlet series with an Euler product, the Hasse–Weil $L$-function of $E$.
Modularity of $E$ gives its meromorphic continuation, so it is an $L$-function in the sense above.
links.why: It shows how arithmetic data of a curve turns into an L-function.

reminder: The space $L^1(\mu)$ holds the integrable functions, with norm $\|f\|_1=\int|f|\,d\mu$.
definition: For a [measure space](c:measure-space) $(X,\mu)$, the space $L^1(\mu)$ is the set of [integrable](c:integrable-function) measurable functions $f:X\to\mathbb{C}$, that is $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$, where functions that agree almost everywhere count as equal. It is a [Banach space](c:banach-space) for the [norm](c:norm) $\|f\|_1=\int|f|\,d\mu$.
examples: $L^1([0,1])$ with Lebesgue measure contains every continuous function on $[0,1]$.
$L^1(\mathbb{N})$ with counting measure is the space $\ell^1$ of absolutely summable sequences.
The function $x^{-1/2}$ is in $L^1((0,1])$, although it is unbounded, because $\int_0^1x^{-1/2}dx=2$.
Non-example: $1/x$ is not in $L^1((0,1])$, because $\int_0^1dx/x=\infty$.

steps: Start with the [Lp space](c:lp-space) $L^p(\mu)$ of functions with $\int|f|^p\,d\mu<\infty$, for a real number $p\ge1$.
Put $p=1$, so the condition becomes $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$.
The norm $(\int|f|^p\,d\mu)^{1/p}$ becomes $\int|f|\,d\mu$.
Hence $L^1(\mu)$ is the case $p=1$ of $L^p(\mu)$.
links.why: It shows that results about Lp spaces apply to $L^1$ with $p=1$.

To minimize $x^2+y^2$ subject to $x+y=1$, solve $(2x,2y)=\lambda(1,1)$ to get $x=y=1/2$ and $\lambda=1$.

reminder: The Laplace–Beltrami operator sends a function $f$ on a Riemannian manifold to the divergence of its gradient.
definition: On a [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) $(M,g)$, the Laplace–Beltrami operator sends a [smooth function](c:smooth-function) $f$ to $\Delta f=\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{grad}f)$, with the [divergence](c:divergence) and the [gradient](c:gradient) taken for $g$. In local coordinates, $\Delta f=\frac1{\sqrt{|g|}}\partial_i\big(\sqrt{|g|}\,g^{ij}\partial_jf\big)$. Some authors use the opposite sign.
examples: On $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the Euclidean metric, $\Delta f=\sum_i\partial_i^2f$.
On the unit circle with angle $\theta$, $\Delta f=\partial_\theta^2f$.
On the unit sphere with colatitude $\theta$ and longitude $\varphi$, $\Delta f=\frac1{\sin\theta}\partial_\theta(\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta f)+\frac1{\sin^2\theta}\partial_\varphi^2f$.
Non-example: the sum $\partial_r^2f+\partial_\theta^2f$ in polar coordinates is not the Laplace–Beltrami operator of the plane, because it ignores the metric coefficients.

steps: Take $M=\mathbb{R}^n$ with the Euclidean metric, so $g_{ij}=\delta_{ij}$ and $\sqrt{|g|}=1$.
The coordinate formula becomes $\Delta f=\sum_i\partial_i\partial_if$.
This is the [Laplace operator](c:laplace-operator) of $\mathbb{R}^n$.
links.why: It shows that the Laplace operator is the Laplace–Beltrami operator of flat space.

reminder: A lattice homomorphism is a map between lattices that preserves binary joins and binary meets.
definition: A map $f:L\to M$ between [lattices](c:lattice) is a lattice homomorphism when $f(a\vee b)=f(a)\vee f(b)$ and $f(a\wedge b)=f(a)\wedge f(b)$ for all $a,b\in L$. It need not preserve a top or a bottom element, and every lattice homomorphism is monotone.
examples: For a map $h:X\to Y$, the preimage map $B\mapsto h^{-1}(B)$ from subsets of $Y$ to subsets of $X$ preserves unions and intersections, so it is a lattice homomorphism.
On a chain such as $\mathbb{R}$, every monotone map $\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is a lattice homomorphism, because joins are maxima and meets are minima.
Non-example: the cardinality map $A\mapsto|A|$ from the subsets of $\{1,2\}$ to the chain $\{0,1,2\}$ is monotone but not a lattice homomorphism, because $|\{1\}\cup\{2\}|=2\ne\max(1,1)$.

steps: A lattice is a set with two binary operations, the join $\vee$ and the meet $\wedge$.
A homomorphism of such structures is a map that commutes with all the operations.
So a lattice homomorphism is a map that commutes with $\vee$ and with $\wedge$.
links.why: It shows that a lattice homomorphism is the usual notion of homomorphism for two operations.

steps: Start with a lattice homomorphism $f:L\to M$ between lattices with top elements $\top$ and bottom elements $\bot$.
Add the condition $f(\top)=\top$.
Add the condition $f(\bot)=\bot$.
Then $f$ is a [bounded lattice homomorphism](c:bounded-lattice-hom).
links.why: It shows what a bounded lattice homomorphism adds: it also keeps the top and the bottom.

reminder: The limit inferior of a real sequence is the limit of the infima of its tails.
definition: For a [sequence](c:sequence) $(a_n)$ of [real numbers](c:real-number), the limit inferior is $\liminf_{n\to\infty}a_n=\lim_{n\to\infty}\inf_{k\ge n}a_k=\sup_n\inf_{k\ge n}a_k$, a value in $[-\infty,\infty]$. The infima $\inf_{k\ge n}a_k$ do not decrease as $n$ grows, so the [limit](c:limit-of-a-sequence) always exists, and the second form uses the [supremum](c:least-upper-bound).
examples: For $a_n=(-1)^n$, $\liminf a_n=-1$ and $\limsup a_n=1$.
For a convergent sequence, $\liminf a_n=\lim a_n$.
For $a_n=n$, $\liminf a_n=+\infty$.
Non-example: for $a_1=-5$ and $a_n=1$ when $n\ge2$, the infimum of the sequence is $-5$, but $\liminf a_n=1$, so the limit inferior is not the infimum.

reminder: A point $x$ is a limit point of a set $A$ when every neighborhood of $x$ contains a point of $A$ other than $x$.
definition: Let $A$ be a [subset](c:subset) of a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$. A point $x\in X$ is a limit point of $A$ when every [neighborhood](c:neighborhood) of $x$ contains a point of $A$ that differs from $x$. The set of all limit points of $A$ is the [derived set](c:derived-set) of $A$.
examples: Every point of $[0,1]$ is a limit point of $(0,1)$, including $0$ and $1$.
The point $0$ is a limit point of $\{1/n:n\ge1\}$, although $0$ is not in the set.
Non-example: $1$ is not a limit point of $\{1/n:n\ge1\}$, because the neighborhood $(0.9,1.1)$ contains no point of the set other than $1$.

reminder: A linear combination of vectors $v_1,\dots,v_n$ is a sum $a_1v_1+\dots+a_nv_n$ with scalar coefficients $a_i$.
definition: Let $V$ be a [vector space](c:vector-space) over a [field](c:field) $K$, or more generally a [module](c:module) over a [ring](c:ring). A linear combination of $v_1,\dots,v_n\in V$ is a vector $a_1v_1+\dots+a_nv_n$ with [scalars](c:scalar) $a_1,\dots,a_n\in K$. For an infinite family, only finite sums are allowed, with all but finitely many coefficients equal to zero.
examples: In $\mathbb{R}^2$, $(3,2)=3(1,0)+2(0,1)$ is a linear combination of $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$.
In the space of polynomials, $2+3x-x^2$ is a linear combination of $1$, $x$ and $x^2$.
The zero vector is a linear combination of every family, with all coefficients equal to zero.
Non-example: $(0,0,1)$ is not a linear combination of $(1,0,0)$ and $(0,1,0)$, because every such combination has third coordinate $0$.

reminder: A list over a set $A$ is a finite ordered sequence $(a_1,\dots,a_n)$ of elements of $A$, with repeats allowed.
definition: A list over a [set](c:set) $A$ is a finite sequence $(a_1,\dots,a_n)$ of elements of $A$, where the length $n$ is a [natural number](c:natural-number) and may be $0$. Order and repeats matter, so $(a,b)\ne(b,a)$ and $(a,a)\ne(a)$. Equivalently, a list is either empty or an element followed by a list.
examples: $(2,3,2)$ is a list of natural numbers of length $3$, and it differs from $(3,2,2)$ and from $(2,3)$.
A [word](c:word) over an alphabet $A$ is a list of letters of $A$.
The empty list $()$ is a list over every set.
Non-example: the set $\{2,3\}$ is not a list, because a set ignores order and repeats.

reminder: A rewriting relation is locally confluent when two one-step reducts of the same element always have a common reduct.
definition: Let $\to$ be a binary relation on a [set](c:set) $X$, that is an [abstract rewriting system](c:abstract-rewriting-system), and write $\to^*$ for its reflexive-transitive closure. The relation is locally confluent when $a\to b$ and $a\to c$ always give an element $d$ with $b\to^*d$ and $c\to^*d$.
examples: A relation in which every element has at most one one-step successor, such as $n\to n-1$ on the positive integers, is locally confluent.
On $\mathbb{N}$, put $n\to n+1$ and $n\to n+2$; the reducts $n+1$ and $n+2$ of $n$ meet at $n+2$, so the relation is locally confluent.
Non-example: on $\{a,b,c\}$ with only $a\to b$ and $a\to c$, the elements $b$ and $c$ have no common reduct, so the relation is not locally confluent.

steps: Let $\to$ be a [confluent relation](c:confluent-relation): whenever $a\to^*b$ and $a\to^*c$, some $d$ has $b\to^*d$ and $c\to^*d$.
Take single steps $a\to b$ and $a\to c$.
A single step is a path of length one, so $a\to^*b$ and $a\to^*c$.
By confluence, $b$ and $c$ have a common reduct, so the relation is locally confluent; the converse needs termination.
links.why: It shows that confluence is the strong form of local confluence, and that Newman's lemma closes the gap for terminating relations.

reminder: A locally presentable category is cocomplete and has a set of small objects that generates every object by filtered colimits.
definition: A [category](c:category) $\mathcal C$ is locally presentable when it is [cocomplete](c:cocomplete-category) and, for some regular [cardinal](c:cardinal-number) $\lambda$, it has a set $S$ of $\lambda$-presentable objects such that every object is a $\lambda$-[filtered colimit](c:filtered-colimit) of objects of $S$. An object $A$ is $\lambda$-presentable when $\mathrm{Hom}(A,-)$ preserves $\lambda$-filtered colimits.
examples: The categories of sets, groups, abelian groups, rings and modules over a ring are locally presentable.
Every category of presheaves $[\mathcal C^{op},\mathbf{Set}]$ on a small category $\mathcal C$ is locally presentable, for example the category of simplicial sets.
Non-example: the category of finite sets is not locally presentable, because it is not cocomplete: it has no infinite coproducts.

steps: Take a locally finitely presentable category: it is cocomplete and generated by finitely presentable objects under filtered colimits.
Finitely presentable means $\aleph_0$-presentable, so the cardinal $\lambda=\aleph_0$ works.
So the category satisfies the definition with $\lambda=\aleph_0$.
The general case lets $\lambda$ be any regular cardinal.
links.why: It shows that locally presentable categories allow larger cardinals than the finitary case.

steps: An [accessible category](c:accessible-category) has, for some regular $\lambda$, $\lambda$-filtered colimits and a set of $\lambda$-presentable objects that generates it.
A locally presentable category has these two properties, so it is accessible.
The locally presentable case adds that the category is [cocomplete](c:cocomplete-category).
links.why: It shows that a locally presentable category is an accessible category that is also cocomplete.

reminder: A quantity or law is Lorentz invariant when every Lorentz transformation leaves it unchanged.
definition: The [Lorentz group](c:lorentz-group) acts on [Minkowski space](c:minkowski-space) by the linear maps $\Lambda$ that preserve the [Minkowski metric](c:minkowski-metric). A function $f$ is Lorentz invariant when $f(\Lambda x)=f(x)$ for every such $\Lambda$, and a set of equations is Lorentz invariant when every $\Lambda$ sends solutions to solutions. A theory is Lorentz invariant when its laws have this property, so the laws are the same in every inertial frame.
examples: The spacetime interval $-t^2+x^2+y^2+z^2$ is Lorentz invariant.
Maxwell's equations in vacuum and the Klein-Gordon equation $(\Box+m^2)\phi=0$ are Lorentz invariant.
Non-example: the time coordinate $t$ is not Lorentz invariant, because a boost with speed $v$ gives $t'=\gamma(t-vx)$.

reminder: A Lorentzian manifold is a smooth manifold with a metric of signature $(-,+,\dots,+)$ on every tangent space.
definition: A Lorentzian manifold is a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $M$ with a smooth [pseudo-Riemannian metric](c:pseudo-riemannian-metric) $g$ of Lorentzian [signature](c:signature-of-a-metric). At every point, $g$ is a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form on $T_pM$ with one negative and $n-1$ positive eigenvalues, and some authors use the opposite sign.
examples: Minkowski space $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $g=-dt^2+dx_1^2+\dots+dx_{n-1}^2$ is a Lorentzian manifold.
For a Riemannian manifold $(N,h)$, the product $\mathbb{R}\times N$ with metric $-dt^2+h$ is a Lorentzian manifold.
The Schwarzschild spacetime and the de Sitter spacetime are Lorentzian manifolds.
Non-example: a Riemannian manifold is not Lorentzian, because its metric is positive definite; a metric with signature $(-,-,+,+)$ is not Lorentzian either.

steps: A [pseudo-Riemannian manifold](c:pseudo-riemannian-manifold) has a smooth, symmetric, nondegenerate metric of constant signature.
A Lorentzian metric is smooth, symmetric and nondegenerate.
Its signature has one negative sign and $n-1$ positive signs at every point, so it is constant.
So $M$ is pseudo-Riemannian; the Lorentzian case adds that exactly one direction is negative.
links.why: It shows that Lorentzian geometry is pseudo-Riemannian geometry with one time direction.

steps: Take $\mathbb{R}^d$ with the constant metric $\eta=\mathrm{diag}(-1,1,\dots,1)$.
The metric $\eta$ is smooth, symmetric and nondegenerate, with one negative eigenvalue.
So $(\mathbb{R}^d,\eta)$ is a Lorentzian manifold, and it is flat [Minkowski space](c:minkowski-space).
links.why: It shows that Minkowski space is the flat model among Lorentzian manifolds.

steps: Start with a time-oriented Lorentzian manifold $M$.
Add the condition that $M$ has a [Cauchy surface](c:cauchy-surface), a set that every inextendible timelike curve meets exactly once.
Then $M$ is a [globally hyperbolic Lorentzian manifold](c:globally-hyperbolic-lorentzian-manifold).
links.why: It shows that global hyperbolicity is one extra causal condition on a Lorentzian manifold.

reminder: A function $f$ is lower semicontinuous when $f(x)\le\liminf_{y\to x}f(y)$ at every point $x$.
definition: A function $f:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}$ on a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is lower semicontinuous when $\{x:f(x)>a\}$ is an [open set](c:open-set) for every real number $a$. Equivalently, $f(x)\le\liminf_{y\to x}f(y)$ at every $x$, where $\liminf$ is the [limit inferior](c:limit-inferior).
examples: Every continuous function is lower semicontinuous.
The indicator function of an open set is lower semicontinuous.
The pointwise supremum of any family of continuous functions is lower semicontinuous.
Non-example: the indicator function $f$ of $[0,1]$ is not lower semicontinuous at $0$, because $\{f>1/2\}=[0,1]$ is not open.

steps: Let $f:X\to\mathbb{R}$ be a [continuous function](c:continuous-function).
For each real number $a$, the set $(a,\infty)$ is open in $\mathbb{R}$.
So the preimage $\{x:f(x)>a\}=f^{-1}((a,\infty))$ is open.
Hence $f$ is lower semicontinuous; continuity also makes the sets $\{f<a\}$ open, which is upper semicontinuity.
links.why: It shows that continuity is lower semicontinuity together with its mirror image, upper semicontinuity.

reminder: A lower set of a preorder is a subset that contains every element below each of its elements.
definition: In a [preorder](c:is-preorder) $(P,\le)$, a [subset](c:subset) $L\subseteq P$ is a lower set when $x\le y$ and $y\in L$ always give $x\in L$. Lower sets are also called down-sets or downward closed sets.
examples: In $(\mathbb{R},\le)$, the rays $(-\infty,a)$ and $(-\infty,a]$ are lower sets.
In the divisibility order on the positive integers, the set of divisors of $12$ is a lower set.
A family of sets that is closed under taking subsets, such as the faces of a simplicial complex, is a lower set of the power set.
Non-example: in $(\mathbb{R},\le)$, the interval $[0,1]$ is not a lower set, because $-1\le0$ and $0\in[0,1]$ but $-1\notin[0,1]$.

reminder: A Lyapunov function for an equilibrium is a positive definite function that does not increase along solutions of the system.
definition:
Let $x^*$ be an equilibrium of the [ordinary differential equation](c:ordinary-differential-equation) $\dot x=F(x)$ on an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$. A Lyapunov function for $x^*$ is a continuously [differentiable function](c:differentiable-function) $V:U	o\mathbb{R}$ with $V(x^*)=0$, $V(x)>0$ for $x
e x^*$, and $\dot V(x)=
abla V(x)\cdot F(x)\le0$ on $U$, where $
abla V$ is the [gradient](c:gradient). Such a function proves [Lyapunov stability](c:lyapunov-stability) of $x^*$, and $\dot V<0$ for $x
e x^*$ proves asymptotic stability.
examples: For $\dot x=-x$ on $\mathbb{R}$ with $x^*=0$, the function $V(x)=x^2$ is a Lyapunov function, because $\dot V=-2x^2\le0$.
For the oscillator $\ddot x=-x$, the energy $V=\tfrac12(x^2+\dot x^2)$ is a Lyapunov function with $\dot V=0$.

For an irreducible [Markov chain](c:markov-chain), a function $V\ge0$ with expected one-step change at most $-\varepsilon<0$ outside a finite set, and finite on that set, shows positive recurrence (Foster).
Non-example: for $\dot x=x$, the function $V(x)=x^2$ is not a Lyapunov function, because $\dot V=2x^2>0$ for $x\ne0$.

reminder: The mapping class group of a surface is the group of isotopy classes of its orientation-preserving homeomorphisms.
definition: For an oriented [surface](c:surface) $S$, the mapping class group $\mathrm{Mod}(S)$ is the [group](c:group) of [isotopy](c:isotopy) classes of orientation-preserving [homeomorphisms](c:homeomorphism) $S\to S$, with composition as product. Equivalently, it is $\pi_0$ of the group $\mathrm{Homeo}^+(S)$. For a surface with boundary or marked points, one usually asks that the maps and the isotopies fix them.
examples: For the torus $T^2$, $\mathrm{Mod}(T^2)\cong SL(2,\mathbb{Z})$.
For the sphere $S^2$, the group of orientation-preserving classes is trivial.
For the annulus with boundary fixed pointwise, the mapping class group is $\mathbb{Z}$, generated by a Dehn twist.
Non-example: the group $\mathrm{Homeo}^+(S)$ is not the mapping class group, because it keeps homeomorphisms that differ by an isotopy as different elements.

reminder: The inverse of a square matrix $A$ is the matrix $B$ with $AB=BA=I$.
definition: Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ [matrix](c:matrix) over a [ring](c:ring). A matrix inverse of $A$ is an $n\times n$ matrix $A^{-1}$ with $AA^{-1}=A^{-1}A=I_n$, where $I_n$ is the [identity matrix](c:identity-matrix). Over a field, $A$ has an inverse exactly when $\det A\ne0$, and then the inverse is unique.
examples: $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}-2&1\\3/2&-1/2\end{pmatrix}$.
A diagonal matrix with nonzero entries $d_i$ has the diagonal matrix with entries $1/d_i$ as its inverse.
A rotation matrix $R_\theta$ has inverse $R_{-\theta}$, which equals its transpose.
Non-example: $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$ has no inverse, because its determinant is $0$.

steps: Square $n\times n$ matrices over a field $K$ form a ring $M_n(K)$ with the matrix product and the unit $I_n$.
An element $a$ of a ring is [invertible](c:invertible) when some $b$ has $ab=ba=1$.
For $a=A$ and $1=I_n$, this condition reads $AB=BA=I_n$.
So the matrix inverse is the inverse of an invertible element of $M_n(K)$.
links.why: It shows that the matrix inverse is the ordinary inverse of a ring element in the ring of matrices.

reminder: The matrix ring $M_n(R)$ is the ring of $n\times n$ matrices over $R$ with entrywise sum and matrix product.
definition: For a [ring](c:ring) $R$ and $n\ge1$, the matrix ring $M_n(R)$ is the set of $n\times n$ [matrices](c:matrix) with entries in $R$, with entrywise addition and the product $(AB)_{ij}=\sum_kA_{ik}B_{kj}$. It has identity $I_n$ when $R$ has an identity, and it is not commutative when $n\ge2$ and $R\ne0$.
examples: $M_2(\mathbb{R})$ is the ring of real $2\times2$ matrices, and it has zero divisors: $E_{12}^2=0$ although $E_{12}\ne0$.
For a field $K$, the ring $M_n(K)$ is the ring of linear maps from $K^n$ to itself.
Non-example: the set of invertible $n\times n$ matrices is not a matrix ring, because it is not closed under addition; it is the group $GL_n$.

steps: Matrix addition is entrywise, so the $n\times n$ matrices form an abelian group under addition.
The matrix product is associative, and it has identity $I_n$ when $R$ has an identity.
The product distributes over addition on both sides.
So $M_n(R)$ is a [ring](c:ring), and it is a noncommutative one when $n\ge2$ and $R\ne0$.
links.why: It shows that matrix rings are the basic noncommutative examples of rings.

reminder: The maximum degree $\Delta(G)$ of a graph $G$ is the largest degree of a vertex of $G$.
definition: For a finite [graph](c:graph) $G$ with at least one vertex, the maximum degree is $\Delta(G)=\max_{v\in V(G)}\deg(v)$, where $\deg(v)$ is the [vertex degree](c:vertex-degree), the number of edges at $v$.
examples: The path on four vertices has $\Delta=2$, and the star $K_{1,n}$ has $\Delta=n$.
The complete graph $K_n$ has $\Delta=n-1$, and every [regular graph](c:regular-graph) of degree $r$ has $\Delta=r$.
Non-example: the average degree is not the maximum degree; in the star $K_{1,3}$ the average degree is $3/2$, but $\Delta=3$.

reminder: The maximum modulus of $f$ on a compact set $K$ is the largest value of $|f(z)|$ for $z\in K$.
definition: For a [continuous function](c:continuous-function) $f$ on a [compact](c:compact-space) set $K\subseteq\mathbb{C}$, the maximum modulus of $f$ on $K$ is $\max_{z\in K}|f(z)|$, the largest value of the [absolute value](c:absolute-value) of $f$. For the circle $|z-a|=r$, one writes $M(r)=\max_{|z-a|=r}|f(z)|$.
examples: For $f(z)=z^2$, the maximum modulus on the circle $|z|=r$ is $M(r)=r^2$.
For $f(z)=e^z$, the maximum modulus on the circle $|z|=r$ is $M(r)=e^r$.
Non-example: on the open unit disc, $f(z)=z$ has supremum $1$ of $|f|$ but no maximum, because the disc is not compact.

reminder: The Mayer–Vietoris sequence is a long exact sequence that relates the homology of $A\cup B$ to that of $A$, $B$ and $A\cap B$.
definition: Let $X=A\cup B$ where the interiors of $A$ and $B$ form an [open cover](c:open-cover) of $X$. The Mayer–Vietoris sequence is the long [exact sequence](c:exact-sequence) $\cdots\to H_n(A\cap B)\to H_n(A)\oplus H_n(B)\to H_n(X)\xrightarrow{\partial}H_{n-1}(A\cap B)\to\cdots$ of [homology](c:homology) groups, with maps induced by inclusions and a connecting map $\partial$. The same pattern holds for cohomology, and for the homotopy groups of a [homotopy pullback](c:homotopy-pullback) square.
examples: Cover $S^1$ by two open arcs that meet in two arcs; both arcs are contractible, so $H_1(S^1)\cong\ker(\mathbb{Z}^2\to\mathbb{Z}^2)\cong\mathbb{Z}$.
Cover $S^n$ by two open sets that deformation retract to hemispheres, with $A\cap B\simeq S^{n-1}$; this gives $\tilde H_k(S^n)\cong\tilde H_{k-1}(S^{n-1})$.
Non-example: the long exact sequence of a pair $(X,A)$ is not a Mayer–Vietoris sequence, because it uses one subspace $A$ and the relative groups $H_n(X,A)$, not a cover by two sets.

steps: Let $C_*(A+B)\subseteq C_*(X)$ be the chains in which every simplex lies in $A$ or in $B$.
The sequence $0\to C_*(A\cap B)\to C_*(A)\oplus C_*(B)\to C_*(A+B)\to0$ of chain complexes is short exact.
A short exact sequence of chain complexes gives a [long exact sequence in homology](c:long-exact-sequence-in-chain-homology).
When the interiors of $A$ and $B$ cover $X$, the inclusion $C_*(A+B)\to C_*(X)$ induces isomorphisms in homology, which gives Mayer–Vietoris.
links.why: It shows where the sequence comes from: a short exact sequence of chain complexes.

reminder: A minimal surface has mean curvature zero at every point, so its area is stationary under all compactly supported variations.
definition: A minimal surface is a [surface](c:surface) immersed in a [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold), for example in $\mathbb{R}^3$, whose mean curvature is zero at every point; the mean curvature is the average of the [principal curvatures](c:principal-curvature). Equivalently, the [area](c:area) of the surface is stationary under every compactly supported variation.
examples: Every plane in $\mathbb{R}^3$ is a minimal surface.
The catenoid and the helicoid are minimal surfaces in $\mathbb{R}^3$.
Non-example: the round sphere in $\mathbb{R}^3$ has constant mean curvature $1/r\ne0$, so it is not minimal.

reminder: Minkowski space is $\mathbb{R}^d$ with the constant metric $-(dx^0)^2+(dx^1)^2+\dots+(dx^{d-1})^2$.
definition: The $d$-dimensional Minkowski space is the [Lorentzian manifold](c:lorentzian-manifold) $\mathbb{R}^d$ with coordinates $(x^0,\dots,x^{d-1})$ and the constant [Minkowski metric](c:minkowski-metric) $\eta=-(dx^0)^2+(dx^1)^2+\dots+(dx^{d-1})^2$. It is flat, and its group of isometries is the [Poincaré group](c:poincare-group).
examples: For $d=4$, Minkowski space is the flat spacetime of special relativity, with $\eta=-dt^2+dx^2+dy^2+dz^2$.
For $d=2$, the light cones are the lines $x^1=\pm x^0$.
Non-example: $\mathbb{R}^4$ with the Euclidean metric is not Minkowski space, because its metric is positive definite.

steps: Take the smooth manifold $\mathbb{R}^d$ with the constant metric $\eta=\mathrm{diag}(-1,1,\dots,1)$.
The metric $\eta$ is smooth, symmetric and nondegenerate.
It has one negative eigenvalue and $d-1$ positive ones, so its signature is Lorentzian.
So $(\mathbb{R}^d,\eta)$ is a [Lorentzian manifold](c:lorentzian-manifold); Minkowski space adds that the metric is constant, so it is flat.
links.why: It shows that Minkowski space is the flat special case of a Lorentzian manifold.

reminder: A model category is a category with weak equivalences, fibrations and cofibrations that satisfy lifting and factorization axioms.
definition: A model category is a [category](c:category) with all small limits and colimits and three classes of maps, the [weak equivalences](c:weak-equivalence), the [fibrations](c:fibration) and the [cofibrations](c:cofibration). The weak equivalences satisfy 2-out-of-3, and all three classes are closed under retracts. Cofibrations have the [lifting property](c:has-lifting-property) against maps that are fibrations and weak equivalences, fibrations have it against maps that are cofibrations and weak equivalences, and every map factors in two ways, as a cofibration followed by a trivial fibration and as a trivial cofibration followed by a fibration.
examples: Topological spaces, with the weak homotopy equivalences, the Serre fibrations and the retracts of relative cell complexes, form a model category (Quillen).
Simplicial sets, with the weak homotopy equivalences, all monomorphisms as cofibrations and the Kan fibrations, form a model category whose fibrant objects are the [Kan complexes](c:kan-complex).
Chain complexes of modules over a ring, with the quasi-isomorphisms and the degreewise surjections as fibrations, form a model category.
Non-example: in the category of sets, the surjections do not form a class of weak equivalences, because 2-out-of-3 fails: $g\circ f$ and $g$ can be surjective while $f$ is not.

steps: Start with a model category $\mathcal M$ with all small limits and colimits.
Add a set $I$ of generating cofibrations and a set $J$ of generating trivial cofibrations.
Require that fibrations have the right lifting property against $J$, trivial fibrations against $I$, and that the domains are small.
Then the small object argument gives the factorizations, and $\mathcal M$ is a [cofibrantly generated model category](c:cofibrantly-generated-model-category).
links.why: It shows what cofibrantly generated model categories add: the model structure comes from two sets of maps.

reminder: The modular group is $PSL(2,\mathbb{Z})$, the integer matrices of determinant one modulo $\pm I$, acting on the upper half plane.
definition: The modular group is $\Gamma=PSL(2,\mathbb{Z})=SL(2,\mathbb{Z})/\{\pm I\}$, the [projective special linear group](c:projective-special-linear-group) over the integers. It acts on the [upper half plane](c:upper-half-plane) by $z\mapsto\frac{az+b}{cz+d}$ for $ad-bc=1$, and some authors call [$SL(2,\mathbb{Z})$](c:sl-2-z) itself the modular group.
examples: The maps $T(z)=z+1$ and $S(z)=-1/z$ generate the modular group.
The modular group has the presentation $\langle S,T\mid S^2=(ST)^3=1\rangle$, so it is isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}/2*\mathbb{Z}/3$.
The set $\{|z|\ge1,\ |\mathrm{Re}\,z|\le1/2\}$ is a fundamental domain for the action on the upper half plane.
Non-example: $PSL(2,\mathbb{R})$ is not the modular group, because its matrices have real entries, not integer entries.

steps: The group $PSL(n,R)$ is $SL(n,R)$ modulo its scalar matrices of determinant one.
Take $n=2$ and $R=\mathbb{Z}$, so the scalar matrices in $SL(2,\mathbb{Z})$ are $\pm I$.
Then the quotient is $PSL(2,\mathbb{Z})=SL(2,\mathbb{Z})/\{\pm I\}$, by the definition of $PSL$.
This quotient is the modular group.
links.why: It shows that the modular group is the projective special linear group of the ring of integers in dimension two.

reminder: A module homomorphism is a map $f:M\to N$ with $f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)$ and $f(rx)=rf(x)$.
definition: Let $M$ and $N$ be left [modules](c:module) over a [ring](c:ring) $R$. A module homomorphism, or $R$-linear map, is a map $f:M\to N$ with $f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)$ and $f(rx)=rf(x)$ for all $x,y\in M$ and $r\in R$.
examples: For a commutative ring $R$ and $a\in R$, the map $x\mapsto ax$ is a module homomorphism $R\to R$.
The reduction map $\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/n$ is a module homomorphism over $\mathbb{Z}$.
Non-example: complex conjugation $\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}$ is $\mathbb{R}$-linear but not $\mathbb{C}$-linear, because $\overline{iz}=-i\bar z\ne i\bar z$.

steps: Start with a [linear map](c:linear-map) $f:V\to W$ between vector spaces over a field $K$.
A field is a ring, and a vector space over $K$ is a module over $K$.
The two linearity conditions are the two conditions of a module homomorphism with $R=K$.
So $f$ is a module homomorphism; the general case lets $R$ be any ring.
links.why: It shows that module homomorphisms extend linear maps from fields to arbitrary rings.

steps: A module is an abelian group under addition.
A module homomorphism $f$ satisfies $f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)$, so it is a [group homomorphism](c:group-homomorphism) of the additive groups.
The module case adds the condition $f(rx)=rf(x)$ for every $r\in R$.
links.why: It shows that a module homomorphism is a group homomorphism that also respects scalars.

reminder: A Möbius transformation is a map $z\mapsto(az+b)/(cz+d)$ of the projective line with $ad-bc\ne0$.
definition: Let $k$ be a [field](c:field) and let $\mathbb{P}^1(k)=k\cup\{\infty\}$ be the [projective line](c:projective-line). A Möbius transformation is a map $f(z)=\frac{az+b}{cz+d}$ of $\mathbb{P}^1(k)$ with $a,b,c,d\in k$ and $ad-bc\ne0$, where $f(\infty)=a/c$, with $f(\infty)=\infty$ when $c=0$, and $f(-d/c)=\infty$ when $c\ne0$. The Möbius transformations form a group under composition, isomorphic to the [projective linear group](c:projective-linear-group) $PGL(2,k)$.
examples: Over $\mathbb{C}$, the translations $z\mapsto z+b$, the maps $z\mapsto az$ with $a\ne0$, and the inversion $z\mapsto1/z$ are Möbius transformations.
The Cayley transform $z\mapsto(z-i)/(z+i)$ maps the upper half plane onto the unit disc.
A Möbius transformation of $\mathbb{C}\cup\{\infty\}$ is determined by the images of three distinct points.
Non-example: $z\mapsto(2z+4)/(z+2)$ is not a Möbius transformation, because $ad-bc=2\cdot2-4\cdot1=0$ and the map is the constant $2$.

steps: A [rational function](c:rational-function) is a quotient $P(z)/Q(z)$ of two polynomials.
Take $P(z)=az+b$ and $Q(z)=cz+d$, which both have degree at most one.
The condition $ad-bc\ne0$ means that $P$ and $Q$ have no common factor and the map is not constant.
So $f$ is a rational function of degree one; the Möbius case adds that $f$ is a bijection of the projective line.
links.why: It shows that Möbius transformations are exactly the invertible rational functions of degree one.

reminder: A monotone scheme is a finite difference scheme whose new value is a nondecreasing function of every old value it uses.
definition: A [finite difference method](c:finite-difference-method) $u_j^{n+1}=H(u_{j-k}^n,\dots,u_{j+k}^n)$ for a [conservation law](c:conservation-law) $u_t+f(u)_x=0$ is monotone when $H$ is a nondecreasing function of each of its arguments. Then $u^n\le v^n$ at all grid points implies $u^{n+1}\le v^{n+1}$ at all grid points, so the scheme is a [monotone](c:monotone-function) map on grid functions.
examples: The Lax–Friedrichs scheme is monotone when the time step satisfies $\frac{\Delta t}{\Delta x}\max|f'|\le1$.

The upwind scheme $u_j^{n+1}=(1-
u)u_j^n+
u u_{j-1}^n$ for $u_t+au_x=0$ with $a>0$ and $
u=a\Delta t/\Delta x$ is monotone when $0\le
u\le1$.

Non-example: the Lax–Wendroff scheme for $u_t+au_x=0$ is not monotone when $0<
u<1$, because the coefficient $
u(
u-1)/2$ of $u_{j+1}^n$ is negative.

steps: A [finite difference method](c:finite-difference-method) computes each new grid value from nearby old values by a formula $H$.
A monotone scheme is such a method.
It adds one condition: $H$ is nondecreasing in each of its arguments.
links.why: It shows that monotonicity is one property of the update formula of a finite difference method.

reminder: Morava E-theory $E_n$ is the complex oriented cohomology theory of the universal deformation of a height $n$ formal group over $\mathbb{F}_{p^n}$.
definition: Morava E-theory $E_n$ at a prime $p$ and height $n\ge1$ is the [complex oriented cohomology theory](c:complex-oriented-cohomology-theory) with coefficients $E_n^*=W(\mathbb{F}_{p^n})[[u_1,\dots,u_{n-1}]][u^{\pm1}]$ in even degrees, where $W$ gives the [Witt vectors](c:ring-of-witt-vectors) and $u$ has degree $2$ or $-2$ by convention. Its [formal group](c:formal-group) is the universal deformation of a formal group of [height](c:height-of-a-formal-group) $n$ over $\mathbb{F}_{p^n}$, and the theory is [Landweber exact](c:landweber-exactness).
examples: For $n=1$, $E_1$ is $p$-complete periodic complex K-theory, with coefficients $\mathbb{Z}_p[u^{\pm1}]$.
The extended Morava stabilizer group acts on $E_n$ by $E_\infty$ ring maps (Goerss–Hopkins–Miller), and homotopy fixed points of its finite subgroups give the spectra [EO(n)](c:eo-n).
Non-example: Morava K-theory $K(n)$ is not Morava E-theory, because its coefficients $\mathbb{F}_p[v_n^{\pm1}]$ are a graded field, not a power series ring over Witt vectors.

reminder: Morava K-theory $K(n)$ at a prime $p$ is a complex oriented cohomology theory with coefficients $\mathbb{F}_p[v_n^{\pm1}]$ and a formal group of height $n$.
definition: Morava K-theory $K(n)$ at a [prime number](c:prime-number) $p$ and height $n\ge1$ is the [complex oriented cohomology theory](c:complex-oriented-cohomology-theory) with $K(n)_*=\mathbb{F}_p[v_n^{\pm1}]$, where $|v_n|=2(p^n-1)$, whose [formal group law](c:formal-group-law) has [height](c:height-of-a-formal-group) $n$. By convention, $K(0)$ is rational cohomology and $K(\infty)$ is cohomology with coefficients in $\mathbb{F}_p$.
examples: At $p=2$, $K(1)$ is mod 2 complex K-theory.
At an odd prime $p$, mod $p$ complex K-theory splits into $p-1$ shifted copies of $K(1)$.
Since $K(n)_*$ is a graded field, $K(n)$ has a Künneth isomorphism $K(n)_*(X\times Y)\cong K(n)_*X\otimes_{K(n)_*}K(n)_*Y$.
Non-example: complex cobordism $MU$ is not $K(n)$, because $MU_*=\mathbb{Z}[x_1,x_2,\dots]$ is not a graded field.

reminder: The mutual information of $X$ and $Y$ is $I(X;Y)=H(X)+H(Y)-H(X,Y)$, the entropy that they share.
definition: For [random variables](c:random-variable) $X,Y$ with joint distribution $p(x,y)$ and marginals $p(x)$ and $p(y)$, the mutual information is $I(X;Y)=\sum_{x,y}p(x,y)\log\frac{p(x,y)}{p(x)p(y)}$. It equals $H(X)+H(Y)-H(X,Y)$ for the [entropy](c:entropy) $H$, and it is the [relative entropy](c:relative-entropy) of the joint distribution from the product of the marginals.
examples: If $X$ and $Y$ are [independent](c:independent-random-variables), then $I(X;Y)=0$.
If $X$ is uniform on $n$ values, then $I(X;X)=H(X)=\log n$.
For a binary symmetric channel with error probability $p$ and a uniform input, $I(X;Y)=1-h(p)$ bits, where $h$ is the binary entropy function.
Non-example: correlation is not mutual information; for $X$ uniform on $\{-1,0,1\}$ and $Y=X^2$, the correlation is $0$ but $I(X;Y)>0$, because $Y$ determines $|X|$.

steps: Let $P_{XY}$ be the joint distribution of $X$ and $Y$, and let $P_X\otimes P_Y$ be the product of its marginals.
The [relative entropy](c:relative-entropy) is $D(P_{XY}\|P_X\otimes P_Y)=\sum p(x,y)\log\frac{p(x,y)}{p(x)p(y)}$.
This sum is the definition of $I(X;Y)$.
So mutual information is the relative entropy of the joint law from the product law.
links.why: It shows that mutual information measures how far two variables are from independence.

reminder: A natural isomorphism is a natural transformation whose components are all isomorphisms.
definition: Let $F,G:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ be [functors](c:functor). A natural isomorphism $\alpha:F\Rightarrow G$ is a [natural transformation](c:natural-transformation) such that every component $\alpha_X:F(X)\to G(X)$ is an [isomorphism](c:isomorphism) in $\mathcal D$. Equivalently, $\alpha$ has an inverse natural transformation $G\Rightarrow F$.
examples: For finite-dimensional vector spaces, the canonical map $V\to V^{**}$ is a natural isomorphism from the identity functor to the double dual functor.
The maps $(a,b)\mapsto(b,a)$ from $A\times B$ to $B\times A$ form a natural isomorphism of functors on pairs of sets.

Non-example: on finite-dimensional real vector spaces, put $\alpha_V=\mathrm{id}_V$ for odd $\dim V$ and $\alpha_V=-\mathrm{id}_V$ for even $\dim V$; every component is an isomorphism, but $\alpha$ is not natural, because $\alpha_{\mathbb{R}^2}f=-f\ne f=f\alpha_{\mathbb{R}}$ for a nonzero map $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^2$.

steps: Start with a [natural transformation](c:natural-transformation) $\alpha:F\Rightarrow G$.
Add the condition that every component $\alpha_X$ is an isomorphism.
Then the inverses $\alpha_X^{-1}$ form a natural transformation $G\Rightarrow F$, so $\alpha$ is invertible among natural transformations.
links.why: It shows that naturality of the inverse needs no separate check.

reminder: The Nevanlinna characteristic $T(r,f)=m(r,f)+N(r,f)$ measures the growth of a meromorphic function $f$ on discs of radius $r$.
definition: For a [meromorphic function](c:meromorphic-function) $f$ on $\mathbb{C}$ and $r>0$, put $m(r,f)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\log^+|f(re^{i\theta})|\,d\theta$ and let $N(r,f)=\int_0^r\frac{n(t,f)-n(0,f)}{t}\,dt+n(0,f)\log r$ be the [logarithmic counting function](c:logarithmic-counting-function) of the poles, where $n(t,f)$ counts the poles in $|z|\le t$ with multiplicity. The Nevanlinna characteristic is $T(r,f)=m(r,f)+N(r,f)$, where $\log^+x=\max(\log x,0)$.
examples: For a polynomial $P$ of degree $d$, $T(r,P)=d\log r+O(1)$.
For $f(z)=e^z$, $T(r,f)=r/\pi$.
Non-example: the [maximum modulus](c:maximum-modulus) is not the Nevanlinna characteristic; for $f(z)=1/(z-1)$ and $r=1$ the maximum modulus is infinite, but $T(1,f)$ is finite.

reminder: A nonnegative function takes only values that are greater than or equal to zero.
definition: A [function](c:function) $f:X\to\mathbb{R}$ with values in the [real numbers](c:real-number) is nonnegative when $f(x)\ge0$ for every $x\in X$. In measure theory, one also allows the value $+\infty$.
examples: The functions $x^2$, $|x|$ and $e^x$ are nonnegative on $\mathbb{R}$.
A probability density function is nonnegative, and so is the indicator function of any set.
Non-example: $\sin x$ is not nonnegative, because $\sin(3\pi/2)=-1$.

reminder: A family of holomorphic functions on an open set is normal when every sequence in it has a locally uniformly convergent subsequence.
definition: A family $\mathcal F$ of [holomorphic functions](c:holomorphic-function) on an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb{C}$ is normal when every sequence in $\mathcal F$ has a [subsequence](c:subsequence) that converges [locally uniformly](c:locally-uniform-convergence) on $U$. Some authors require the limit to be holomorphic, and others also allow the limit $\infty$, measured in the spherical metric.
examples: The family $\{z^n:n\ge1\}$ is normal on the open unit disc, because $z^n\to0$ locally uniformly there.
Every family of holomorphic functions on $U$ that is bounded on each compact subset is normal (Montel).
The family of holomorphic functions on $U$ that omit the values $0$ and $1$ is normal when the limit $\infty$ is allowed (Montel).
Non-example: the family $\{nz:n\ge1\}$ is not normal on a disc around $0$, because $nz\to\infty$ for $z\ne0$ while $nz=0$ at $z=0$.

steps: Give the space $H(U)$ of holomorphic functions on $U$ the [compact-open topology](c:compact-open-topology), the topology of locally uniform convergence.
This topology is metrizable, so a subset is relatively compact when every sequence in it has a subsequence that converges in $H(U)$.
That is exactly normality in the version with holomorphic limits.
So a normal family is a [relatively compact subspace](c:relatively-compact-subspace) of $H(U)$.
links.why: It shows that normality is relative compactness in the right function space, so compactness tools apply.

reminder: The normalizer of a subset $S$ of a group $G$ is the subgroup of elements $g$ with $gSg^{-1}=S$.
definition: For a subset $S$ of a [group](c:group) $G$, the normalizer is $N_G(S)=\{g\in G:gSg^{-1}=S\}$, the set of elements that conjugate $S$ onto itself. It is a [subgroup](c:subgroup) of $G$. When $S=H$ is a subgroup, $N_G(H)$ is the largest subgroup of $G$ that contains $H$ as a [normal subgroup](c:normal-subgroup).
examples: If $G$ is abelian, then $N_G(S)=G$ for every subset $S$.
The normalizer $N_G(H)$ equals $G$ exactly when $H$ is a normal subgroup of $G$.
Non-example: in $S_3$, the element $g=(1\,3)$ is not in $N_G(H)$ for $H=\langle(1\,2)\rangle$, because $gHg^{-1}=\langle(2\,3)\rangle\ne H$.

reminder: The octonions form an 8-dimensional real division algebra with a multiplicative norm, and the product is not associative.
definition: The octonions $\mathbb{O}$ are the 8-dimensional real algebra with basis $1,e_1,\dots,e_7$ that comes from the [quaternions](c:quaternion) $\mathbb{H}$ by the Cayley-Dickson construction, for example $(a,b)(c,d)=(ac-d^*b,\,da+bc^*)$ for $a,b,c,d\in\mathbb{H}$. Its norm $|x|=\sqrt{x\bar x}$ satisfies $|xy|=|x||y|$, so $\mathbb{O}$ is a [normed division algebra](c:normed-division-algebra), and it is [alternative](c:alternative-algebra) but not associative.
examples: The real normed division algebras are $\mathbb{R}$, $\mathbb{C}$, $\mathbb{H}$ and $\mathbb{O}$, of dimensions $1,2,4,8$ (Hurwitz).
For three imaginary units $x,y,z$ with $z$ outside the subalgebra generated by $x$ and $y$, one has $(xy)z=-x(yz)$.
The unit octonions form the sphere $S^7$.
Non-example: the sedenions, the next Cayley-Dickson step, are not octonions, because they have zero divisors.

steps: Take the octonions $\mathbb{O}$, a real algebra with unit.
The norm $|x|=\sqrt{x\bar x}$ satisfies $|xy|=|x||y|$.
This forces $xy=0$ only when $x=0$ or $y=0$, so every nonzero element has an inverse.
So $\mathbb{O}$ is a [normed division algebra](c:normed-division-algebra), the one of dimension $8$, and it is not associative.
links.why: It shows that the octonions are the last of the four real normed division algebras.

reminder: A map between topological spaces is open when it sends every open set to an open set.
definition: A map $f:X\to Y$ between [topological spaces](c:topological-space) is open when, for every [open set](c:open-set) $U\subseteq X$, the [image](c:image) $f(U)$ is an open set of $Y$. An open map need not be continuous.
examples: The projection $\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}$, $(x,y)\mapsto x$, is an open map.
A nonconstant holomorphic function on a connected open set of $\mathbb{C}$ is an open map (open mapping theorem).
Non-example: $x\mapsto x^2$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is continuous but not open, because the image of $(-1,1)$ is $[0,1)$.

steps: Let $f:X\to Y$ be a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism), so $f$ is a bijection and both $f$ and its inverse $g$ are continuous.
For an open set $U\subseteq X$, the image $f(U)$ equals the preimage $g^{-1}(U)$.
The preimage of an open set under the continuous map $g$ is open, so $f(U)$ is open.
So $f$ is an open map; a homeomorphism is a continuous open bijection.
links.why: It shows that a homeomorphism is a bijection that is both continuous and open.

steps: Pass from the spaces to their frames of open sets, with the map $f^{-1}:\mathcal O(Y)\to\mathcal O(X)$.
If $f$ is open, the image map $U\mapsto f(U)$ is left adjoint to $f^{-1}$, because $f(U)\subseteq V$ exactly when $U\subseteq f^{-1}(V)$.
This left adjoint satisfies $f(U\cap f^{-1}V)=f(U)\cap V$, which is Frobenius reciprocity.
So $f$ is an [open morphism](c:open-morphism), the general notion for locales.
links.why: It shows how the topological notion fits into the general notion of an open morphism.

reminder: The operator norm of a bounded linear operator $T$ is $\|T\|=\sup\{\|Tx\|:\|x\|\le1\}$.
definition: For a [bounded linear operator](c:bounded-linear-operator) $T:X\to Y$ between [normed spaces](c:normed-space), the operator norm is $\|T\|=\sup\{\|Tx\|:x\in X,\ \|x\|\le1\}$, the [supremum](c:least-upper-bound) of the output sizes on the unit ball. It is the smallest $C$ with $\|Tx\|\le C\|x\|$ for all $x$.
examples: For a real matrix acting on Euclidean spaces, the operator norm is the largest singular value.
For a diagonal operator on $\ell^2$ with entries $d_i$, the operator norm is $\sup_i|d_i|$.
Non-example: differentiation on polynomials on $[0,1]$ with the sup norm has no operator norm, because $x^n$ has norm $1$ and its derivative has norm $n$.

steps: The bounded linear operators $X\to Y$ form a vector space $B(X,Y)$ with pointwise operations.
The value $\|T\|$ is finite and not negative, and $\|T\|=0$ only when $Tx=0$ for every $x$, that is when $T=0$.
It satisfies $\|aT\|=|a|\|T\|$ and $\|S+T\|\le\|S\|+\|T\|$, because the supremum respects both rules.
So $\|\cdot\|$ is a [norm](c:norm) on $B(X,Y)$.
links.why: It shows that the operator norm turns the space of operators into a normed space.

reminder: An oracle machine is a Turing machine that can ask in one step whether a number belongs to a fixed oracle set.
definition: An oracle machine with oracle $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ is a [Turing machine](c:turing-machine) with an extra oracle tape and three special states: query, yes and no. When the machine enters the query state with the number $n$ on the oracle tape, it moves in one step to the yes state if $n\in A$ and to the no state otherwise.
examples: With oracle $A$, a machine that writes its input $n$ on the oracle tape and outputs the answer decides $A$ itself.
With the halting set as oracle, a machine decides whether a given Turing machine halts on a given input, by one query.
A machine may use the answer to one query to choose its next query.
Non-example: a nondeterministic Turing machine is not an oracle machine, because it chooses between moves and gets no answers from a set.

steps: Start with a [Turing machine](c:turing-machine) $M$.
Give $M$ an oracle tape and the query, yes and no states, but never enter the query state.
The result is an oracle machine for every oracle $A$, and it computes the same function as $M$.
So a Turing machine is an oracle machine that never queries.
links.why: It shows that oracle machines extend Turing machines by one extra operation.

reminder: The $k$-th order statistic of a sample is its $k$-th smallest value.
definition: For real [random variables](c:random-variable) $X_1,\dots,X_n$, the $k$-th order statistic $X_{(k)}$ is the $k$-th smallest of the values $X_1,\dots,X_n$ in the [total order](c:total-order) of $\mathbb{R}$. That is, $X_{(1)}\le X_{(2)}\le\dots\le X_{(n)}$ is the sorted sample.
examples: The first order statistic is the minimum $\min_iX_i$, and the $n$-th is the maximum $\max_iX_i$.
For $n=5$, the sample median is the order statistic $X_{(3)}$.
For independent uniform variables on $[0,1]$, $X_{(k)}$ has the Beta distribution with parameters $k$ and $n-k+1$.
Non-example: the $k$-th value $X_k$ in the original order is not the order statistic $X_{(k)}$; for the data $(3,1,2)$, $X_2=1$ but $X_{(2)}=2$.

reminder: The order topology on a totally ordered set is generated by the open rays $\{x<a\}$ and $\{x>a\}$.
definition: Let $(X,<)$ be a [totally ordered set](c:total-order). The order topology on $X$ is the smallest [topology](c:topological-space) that contains every open ray $\{x:x<a\}$ and $\{x:x>a\}$ for $a\in X$. Its basic open sets are the open intervals $(a,b)$ and the open rays.
examples: On $\mathbb{R}$, the order topology is the usual topology, with the open intervals as basic open sets.
On $\mathbb{N}$, the order topology is discrete, because $\{n\}=(n-1,n+1)$ for $n\ge1$ and $\{0\}=\{x<1\}$.
On $\{0,1,2,\dots,\omega\}$ the order topology makes $\omega$ the limit of the sequence $0,1,2,\dots$.

Non-example: on $Y=[0,1)\cup\{2\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ the subspace topology is not the order topology of $Y$, because $\{2\}$ is open in the subspace topology but every basic neighborhood $(a,2]$ of $2$ in $Y$ meets $[0,1)$.
